newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqis flock to market, say unfraid of an attack.
newsitem.headline: Iraqis flock to market, say unfraid of an attack.

text.p: Iraqis gathered in Bab al-Sharji's flea market in Baghdad on Friday, seemingly unconcerned about an American attack as they hawked radios, furniture, household utensils, bicycles, carpets, and clothes they had spread on the ground.
Carts laden with kerosene stoves, eggs and vegetables offered sandwiches, small boys with cool boxes sold beverages and women vendors squatted at street corners selling cigarettes.
A traffic policeman watched vendors from his rickety Toyota. "No one seems to be afraid of Clinton. It is just like any other day," he said, referring to U.S. President Bill Clinton.
By late afternoon the crowd had swelled to thousands. "Barwaribalal apples, fresh from Kurdistan," shouted a boy carrying a basket full of juicy fruits.

There was hardly a mention among the crowd of an imminent U.S. military strike that may include raids on targets in and around Baghdad by the radar-evading Stealth bombers that arrived in Kuwait on Friday.

"They (Kuwaitis) have shown their ugly face again. We have thrown Americans out of Kurdistan in the north. They invite them to strike us from the south. This not is good-neighbourliness," said Ihsan Abdulkareem, selling books from his private library for a living.

The victory by President Saddam Hussein's new allies of Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) over rivals of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) in the Kurdish north has led to a rise in national feelings despite economic hardships caused by U.N. trade sanctions imposed on Iraq for invading Kuwait in 1990.

News about "the liberation of the north from U.S. lackeys and spies" and measures by Saddam to integrate the Kurdish north -- out of his control for the past six years -- with the rest of the country are prominently highlighted by state-controlled radio and television.
For the person on the street, Saddam has emerged as a hero again.
"Let them (Americans) send more warships and planes. The change of the reality on the ground in Iraq is no longer within their reach," said a university lecturer.

"I don't think America is now in a position to say that it cares for the suffering of the Iraqi people. What Washington did and intends to do is maddness. It froze the oil-for-food deal, primarily meant to help the Iraqi people and see what happened to those who relied on it in northern Iraq," said the lecturer, who did not want to be named.
Most people interviewed by Reuters in Bab al-Sharji said they would go to the roofs to watch any laser-guided bombs to be dropped on Baghdad by U.S. F-117A Stealth fighters.

There were no apparent signs of a country readying itself for war in Baghdad on Friday. In the afternoon, tens of thousands of Moslems headed to mosques for their Friday prayers as preachers and Imams pleaded with the Almighty to punish America.

A government-controlled newspaper on Friday hurled insults at Clinton and Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole, accusing them of escalating tension with Iraq for electoral purposes. Presidential elections will be held in November.
The official al-Iraq said both Clinton and Dole had forgotten all about America's problems, focusing instead on how to punish Iraq.

"Thus, the criminal chapter continues, threats and warnings escalate, warships and Stealth bombers move as if there is nothing left for the American voter to think about but how to kill the Iraqis," the paper said in front-page editorial.
